content.content:
# Reducing Power Consumption The following programming techniques can be used to reduce the power consumption of the Game Boy hardware and extend the life of the batteries. ## Using the HALT Instruction The HALT instruction should be used whenever possible to reduce power consumption. The CPU will remain halted until an interrupt *enabled by [the IE register ($FFFF)](<#FFFF — IE: Interrupt enable>)* is flagged in IF, at which point the interrupt is serviced if IME is enabled, and then execution continues at the instruction immediately following the HALT. Depending on how much CPU time is required by a game, the HALT instruction can extend battery life anywhere from 5% to 50% or possibly more. When waiting for a VBlank event, this would be a BAD example: ```rgbasm .wait ld a, [$FF44] ; LY cp a, 144 jr nz, .wait ``` A better example would be a procedure as shown below. In this case the VBlank interrupt must be enabled, and your VBlank interrupt handler must set `vblank_flag` (a one-byte variable allocated in RAM) to a non-zero value. ```rgbasm ld hl, vblank_flag ; hl = pointer to vblank_flag xor a ; a = 0 .wait halt ; suspend CPU - wait for ANY enabled interrupt cp a, [hl] ; is the vblank_flag still zero? jr z, .wait ; keep waiting if zero ld [hl], a ; set the vblank_flag back to zero ``` The `vblank_flag` variable is used to determine whether the HALT period has been terminated by a VBlank interrupt or by another interrupt. Note though that a VBlank interrupt might happen after the cp instruction and before the jr, in which case the interrupt would go unnoticed by the procedure, which would jump again into a halt. Another possibility is, if your game uses no other interrupt than VBlank (or uses no interrupts), to only enable VBlank interrupts and simply use a HALT instruction, which will only resume main code execution when a VBlank occurs. Remember, when using HALT to wait between VBlanks, that your interrupt handlers MUST enable interrupts (using EI before returning, or better, using the RETI instruction) ## Using the STOP Instruction The STOP instruction is intended to switch the Game Boy into VERY low power standby mode. For example, a program may use this feature when it hasn't sensed keyboard input for a longer period (for example, when somebody forgot to turn off the Game Boy). No licensed rom makes use of STOP outside of CGB speed switching. Special care needs to be taken if you want to make use of the STOP instruction. On a DMG, disabling the LCD before invoking STOP leaves the LCD enabled, drawing a horizontal black line on the screen and very likely damaging the hardware. On CGB, leaving the LCD enabled when invoking STOP will result in a black screen. Except if the LCD is in Mode 3, where it will keep drawing the current screen. STOP is terminated by one of the P10 to P13 lines going low. For this reason, d-pad and/or button inputs should be enabled by writing $00, $10 or $20 to the `P1` register before entering STOP (depending on which buttons you want to terminate the STOP on). ### The bizarre case of the Game Boy STOP instruction, before even considering timing. The Game Boy STOP instruction is weird. Normally, it should enter STOP mode, where the CPU sits idle until a button is pressed. The STOP instruction was reused on the Game Boy Color to trigger a CPU speed switch, so executing STOP after writing 1 to KEY1 normally causes a speed switch. STOP is normally a 2-byte instruction where the second byte is ignored. *But the Game Boy isn't normal. Depending on various factors, the STOP instruction might do different things. Will it actually enter STOP mode? Will it enter HALT mode instead? Will it just be a NOP? Will it perform the speed switch I requested? Will it magically become a 1-byte opcode and execute its second byte as another opcode? Will it glitch the CPU in a non-deterministic fashion? Follow the chart to figure out!*


Source: Lior Halphon

## Disabling the Sound Controller If your program doesn't use sound at all (or during some periods) then write $00 to register FF26 to save 16% or more on GB power consumption. Sound can be turned back on by writing $80 to the same register, all sound registers must be then re-initialized. When the Game Boy is turned on, sound is enabled by default, and must be turned off manually when not used. ## Not using CGB Double Speed Mode Because CGB Double Speed mode consumes more power, it's recommended to use normal speed when possible. There's limited ability to switch between both speeds, for example, a game might use normal speed in the title screen, and double speed in the game, or vice versa. However, during speed switch, the display collapses for a short moment, so it's not a good idea to alter speeds within active game or title screen periods. ## Using the Skills Most of the above power saving methods will produce best results when using efficient and tight assembler code which requires as little CPU power as possible. Using a high level language will require more CPU power and these techniques will not have as big as an effect. To optimize your code, it might be a good idea to look at [WikiTI's Z80 Optimization page](https://wikiti.brandonw.net/index.php?title=Z80_Optimization) (although it applies to the original Z80 CPU, so one must adapt the optimizations to the SM83), or at [this SM83-specific page](https://github.com/pret/pokecrystal/wiki/Optimizing-assembly-code). # CPU Instruction Set :::tip If you are looking for textual explanations of what each each instruction does, please read [gbz80(7)](https://rgbds.gbdev.io/docs/gbz80.7); if you want a compact reference card/cheat sheet of each opcode and its flag effects, please consult [the optables](https://gbdev.io/gb-opcodes/optables) (whose [octal view](https://gbdev.io/gb-opcodes/optables/octal) makes most encoding patterns more apparent). ::: The Game Boy's SM83 processor possesses a CISC, variable-length instruction set. This page attempts to shed some light on how the CPU decodes the raw bytes fed into it into instructions. The first byte of each instruction is typically called the "opcode" (for "operation code"). By noticing that some instructions perform identical operations but with different parameters, they can be grouped together; for example, `inc bc`, `inc de`, `inc hl`, and `inc sp` differ only in what 16-bit register they modify. In each table, one line represents one such grouping. Since many groupings have some variation, the variation has to be encoded in the instruction; for example, the above four instructions will be collectively referred to as `inc r16`. Here are the possible placeholders and their values: {{#bits 8 < "r8" 0:"b" 1:"c" 2:"d" 3:"e" 4:"h" 5:"l" 6:"[hl]" 7:"a" ; "r16" 0:"bc" 1:"de" 2:"hl" 3:"sp" ; "r16stk" 0:"bc" 1:"de" 2:"hl" 3:"af" ; "r16mem" 0:"bc" 1:"de" 2:"hl+" 3:"hl-" ; "cond" 0:"nz" 1:"z" 2:"nc" 3:"c" ; "b3" 0-7:"A 3-bit bit index" ; "tgt3" 0-7:"rst's target address, divided by 8" ; "imm8" 0-7:"The following byte" ; "imm16" 0-7:"The following two bytes, in little-endian order" ; }} These last two are a little special: if they are present in the instruction's mnemonic, it means that the instruction is 1 (`imm8`) / 2 (`imm16`) extra bytes long. :::tip `[hl+]` and `[hl-]` can also be notated `[hli]` and `[hld]` respectively (as in **i**ncrement and **d**ecrement). ::: Groupings have been loosely associated based on what they do into separate tables; those have no particular ordering, and are purely for readability and convenience. Finally, the instruction "families" have been further grouped into four "blocks", differentiated by the first two bits of the opcode. ## Block 0 {{#bits 8 > "nop" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5:"0" 4:"0" 3:"0" 2:"0" 1:"0" 0:"0" }} {{#bits 8 > "ld r16, imm16" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5-4:"Dest (r16)" 3:"0" 2:"0" 1:"0" 0:"1" ; "ld [r16mem], a" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5-4:"Dest (r16mem)" 3:"0" 2:"0" 1:"1" 0:"0" ; "ld a, [r16mem]" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5-4:"Source (r16mem)" 3:"1" 2:"0" 1:"1" 0:"0" ; "ld [imm16], sp" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5:"0" 4:"0" 3:"1" 2:"0" 1:"0" 0:"0" ; }} {{#bits 8 > "inc r16" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5-4:"Operand (r16)" 3:"0" 2:"0" 1:"1" 0:"1" ; "dec r16" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5-4:"Operand (r16)" 3:"1" 2:"0" 1:"1" 0:"1" ; "add hl, r16" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5-4:"Operand (r16)" 3:"1" 2:"0" 1:"0" 0:"1" ; }} {{#bits 8 > "inc r8" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5-3:"Operand (r8)" 2:"1" 1:"0" 0:"0" ; "dec r8" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5-3:"Operand (r8)" 2:"1" 1:"0" 0:"1" ; }} {{#bits 8 > "ld r8, imm8" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5-3:"Dest (r8)" 2:"1" 1:"1" 0:"0" }} {{#bits 8 > "rlca" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5:"0" 4:"0" 3:"0" 2:"1" 1:"1" 0:"1" ; "rrca" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5:"0" 4:"0" 3:"1" 2:"1" 1:"1" 0:"1" ; "rla" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5:"0" 4:"1" 3:"0" 2:"1" 1:"1" 0:"1" ; "rra" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5:"0" 4:"1" 3:"1" 2:"1" 1:"1" 0:"1" ; "daa" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5:"1" 4:"0" 3:"0" 2:"1" 1:"1" 0:"1" ; "cpl" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5:"1" 4:"0" 3:"1" 2:"1" 1:"1" 0:"1" ; "scf" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5:"1" 4:"1" 3:"0" 2:"1" 1:"1" 0:"1" ; "ccf" 7:"0" 6:"0" 5:"1" 4:"1" 3:"1" 2:"1" 1:"1" 0:"1" ;

content.thinking:
With the 18-EI sequence starting at 0x1A0, the serial interrupt is pending, and since EI has a one-instruction delay, IME only becomes true after the second EI at 0x1A1, so the interrupt dispatches right after with return address 0x1A2 — meaning BC ends up as 0x01A2 once popped. That matches my model where the enable from the first EI takes effect after the second EI executes.

Now I'm worried about whether ei_pending carries over incorrectly: if EI#2 re-arms ei_pending during dispatch, then the handler's first instruction (pop bc) would itself set IME=1 immediately, making the handler interruptible one instruction early. In this test it doesn't matter since the serial IF was already acknowledged, but it's a real correctness risk for handler atomicity in general. Since Pan Docs doesn't clarify this edge case, I'll make the dispatch authoritative by clearing ei_pending whenever an interrupt is dispatched, which is the safer interpretation.

Same reasoning applies at the handler's start, so clearing on dispatch resolves it either way. I'm checking HALT with EI pending: if an interrupt is already pending when HALT executes, the halt bug triggers with IME=1, so the vblank test case should push the halt address and jump correctly since IF is cleared beforehand. Now I'm ready to write the actual execute function, making it generic and inlined for performance.

Writing CPU helper functions...

Still writing register accessors...

Still writing ALU dispatch logic...

Still writing opcode handlers...

Finishing the rotate/flag instructions and handling Halt, I'm checking the EI+HALT interaction carefully: since IME is still false when HALT executes, pending interrupts trigger the halt bug, otherwise the CPU halts and IME becomes true right after via the delayed EI effect.

Writing instruction dispatch logic...

Still writing opcode handlers...

Finishing the remaining opcodes for calls, pushes, resets, and the illegal opcode handler that locks the CPU.

I'm checking that pushing self.pc works fine with two-phase borrows, then starting on the CB-prefixed instruction decoder, beginning with rotate operations that read a register, compute flags, and write the result back.

Still writing CB decoder... adding bit/res/set cases.

I'm verifying the memory access timing patterns for CB opcodes operating on (HL) match the expected read/write cycle sequence, then thinking about how the pending EI flag interacts with DI during the step function, and starting to consider the illegal opcode lockup case.

Now I'm turning to the dispatch function itself, which resets IME and EI-pending flags at the start, then handles the HALT bug case by decrementing PC when a halt bug condition is active before performing the standard idle bus cycles.

Continuing dispatch logic, I push PCH to the stack, check the pending interrupt bitmap after that write (since modifying IE mid-sequence can affect which interrupt is serviced), push PCL, then compute the vector based on the lowest set pending bit and acknowledge it—defaulting to 0x0000 if nothing remains pending. But I realize I need to double check the ordering: the vector decision needs to happen correctly relative to the PCL write and the ack call.

I'm reasoning through whether sampling pending/acking right at decision time versus right before PCL write would differ, concluding the only edge case is if the PCL write itself targets IF at 0xFF0F, which is negligible—so I'll ack at the decision point. This matches the ie_push test's expected ordering where PCH write happens mid-cycle, pending is sampled after it, and PCL write occurs afterward in the following cycle.

Then I confirm the halted CPU behavior: with IME enabled, a pending interrupt wakes the CPU and dispatches immediately; with IME disabled, a pending interrupt just wakes it into normal fetch-execute.

For persistence, I'm writing the CPU's save/load snapshot methods that serialize all registers, flags, and internal state flags like halted, ei_pending, and halt_bug, with validation on load to reject corrupt flag states, plus I'm planning to add some public helper methods.

I'll also add pub getters for the combined register pairs since they're useful for debugging, then move on to writing cpu.rs with timing documentation in the comments.

For illegal opcodes, I need to confirm each one locks the CPU: a single Read log entry, then subsequent steps produce only Idle with the PC frozen, even with interrupts pending. All tests are passing and clippy is clean, so before committing T14 I want to double-check a couple of deeper correctness edge cases. First, HALT with IME=1 and a pending interrupt correctly wakes and dispatches, pushing PC = X+1 as expected. Now I'm checking the trickier case of EI immediately followed by HALT, since the delayed EI effect could interact oddly with halt state.

I also confirm the halted-wake-with-IME=0 path adds no extra cycles, and that waking from HALT with IME=1 matches Mooneye's halt_ime1_timing2-GS expectation of identical timing to a NOP-serviced interrupt. There's a subtler question though: since peripherals tick before memory access in my ordering, an interrupt raised during the final M-cycle of an instruction becomes visible right at that cycle's end — I need to verify this matches how real hardware times interrupt recognition at the last M-cycle before the next opcode fetch.

This is really the domain Blargg's and Mooneye's intr_timing/di_timing tests probe, and my global ordering switch is the lever to get it right. I'm satisfied the pending() check in HALT and the stop() call after the fetch cycle are both placed correctly, and that the derived PartialEq/Eq on Cpu is harmless. For performance, I'm considering whether a quick micro-benchmark with a tight loop over a FlatBus-backed program would be worth writing, though setting up a throwaway test binary outside my allowed paths is awkward.

I could create a temporary benchmark test file within my cpu* path pattern, run it, then delete it, using a minimal non-logging bus to rule out the Vec push in FlatBus dominating the timing.

All four tasks (T10, T12, T11, and the CPU side of T14) are done and committed on `lane/core`. `cargo test -p gb-core` passes and SST passes 500/500 files, with HALT (76) and STOP (10) only partly checked as listed below. Every commit builds and passes tests on its own, so you can merge any of them. The main repo is untouched (`git -C $REPO status --short` is empty).

## Changed files
All under `/Users/skyseek/Desktop/project/open/research-platform/GB-emulator-lanes/core/crates/core/`, all within my exclusive paths:
- `src/cpu.rs`, `src/decode.rs`, `src/alu.rs`
- `tests/opcode_table.rs`, `tests/sst.rs`, `tests/alu.rs`, `tests/cpu_interrupts.rs`, `tests/cpu_state.rs`
- `tests/cpu_common.rs`: shared test support (a small JSON parser and a 64 KiB flat-RAM fake bus that logs every access). It also builds as its own small test target; the other tests pull it in with `#[path]`.

## Commands and output
`cd $W && CARGO_TARGET_DIR=$W/target CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=3 GBEMU_REFS=$REFS cargo test -p gb-core -- --nocapture`
```
unittests src/lib.rs      test result: ok. 4 passed
tests/alu.rs              test result: ok. 21 passed
tests/cpu_common.rs       test result: ok. 2 passed
tests/cpu_interrupts.rs   test result: ok. 21 passed
tests/cpu_state.rs        test result: ok. 5 passed
tests/opcode_table.rs     test result: ok. 10 passed; 0 ignored
SST: 500/500 files passed (500000 cases); partial-check exceptions: ["10", "76"]
tests/sst.rs              test result: ok. 4 passed; finished in 0.64s
```
- SST passed on the first run with no CPU fixes needed.
- A self-test feeds the SST harness deliberately wrong expectations (wrong PC, F, RAM, access kind, address, cycle count, EI flag) and confirms each one is caught.
- With `GBEMU_REFS` pointing at a missing directory, the SST test prints `SKIP` and passes.
- `SST_ONLY="cb 46,00"` runs just those files (2/2).
- The flag test is no longer ignored; it covers all 500 opcodes with 4 starting flag values and 8 register seeds each.

## Exceptions (for DECISIONS)
- **76 HALT:** SST expects 3 M-cycles. Mine takes 1, matching Opcodes.json; each later step while halted is 1 idle. The test still checks registers, RAM and the opcode fetch, but not the cycle count.
- **10 STOP:** SST expects PC+1 and 3 M-cycles. Mine is 2 bytes and 1 M-cycle (the second byte is skipped without a read) and calls `bus.stop()`, following Pan Docs, gbz80(7) and Opcodes.json. The test checks everything except PC and the cycle count. STOP does not enter a low-power mode; it acts as a 2-byte NOP.

## Additions to frozen types (no signature changes, per D001)
- `Cpu` has three new public fields: `ei_pending` (needed to check SST's `ei`), `halt_bug` and `locked`.
- `Cpu` also gains `af/bc/de/hl` and matching setters (`set_af` clears F's low nibble), and now derives `PartialEq, Eq`.
- `Snapshot for Cpu` starts with the tag `CPU ` and saves every field. Loading rejects a bad tag, truncated data, or a nonzero F low nibble, and leaves the CPU unchanged on failure.

## Behaviour choices
- **EI:** it takes effect after the next instruction, unless that instruction is DI.
- **EI then interrupt:** a dispatch also cancels a pending EI, so an interrupt handler's first instruction can't turn IME back on.
- **EI; HALT with an interrupt pending:** this triggers the HALT bug; the dispatch then pushes the HALT's own address, as Pan Docs describes.
- **Vector timing:** the dispatch picks its vector after writing PCH. If that write clears the pending bit in IE, PC goes to 0x0000 and IF is left alone (the optional Mooneye `ie_push` behaviour is included).
- **Wake-up:** coming out of HALT adds no extra cycle. A test confirms the timing matches a loop of NOPs.

## Open issues
- When an interrupt raised during an instruction's last M-cycle gets serviced depends on D002's peripheral-then-access order. If instr_timing or mem_timing disagree in T30, the fix is the one global switch in the Bus, not the CPU.
- For speed, a throwaway benchmark (deleted afterwards) measured the CPU alone at about 230 M instructions/s, so it won't limit frame rate.

I'm tracing through the second case of the rewrite-timing test: writing 0x12 produces 160 ticks where the first tick is a delay and subsequent ticks transfer bytes 0 through 158, confirming byte 158 lands at tick 159. Then I check what happens when 0x56 is written mid-cycle — the next tick still outputs the pending byte 159 from the old transfer, and only after that does the new value take effect, producing (0x5600, 0) on the following tick.

Now I'm fixing an incorrect comment that describes which cycle the write happens in, correcting it to say the write occurs during the cycle moving byte 158, where the delay cycle afterward still moves the final byte 159 of the old transfer.

Writing the DMA test ROM...

I'm checking that the source data pattern at 0x2000 fills correctly, and tracing the exact cycle timing to confirm the OAM read during DMA lands on byte 0xFF, consistent with the transfer window.

I also want assertions confirming FF46 reads back the triggered value, OAM matches the expected pattern across all 160 bytes, and that running the machine for enough steps reaches the LD B,B breakpoint without issue. I'm also considering a second test variant that sources the DMA from WRAM instead of ROM, to verify the E000-FF00 echo mapping works correctly too.

One ROM-based test should suffice here—adding a WRAM-source variant or a mid-DMA save_state check feels like unnecessary complexity since the DMA snapshot logic already has its own unit test.

content.thinking:
For item 3, I'm working out the w4/core branch change around interrupt check timing. The current model checks interrupts at the start of a step before fetching, but I'm considering shifting it so the opcode fetch happens during the last M-cycle of the current instruction, with the interrupt check occurring right after that fetch—meaning an interrupt raised by a peripheral during that window could affect timing differently.

I'm mapping this onto the SM83's actual overlapped fetch behavior: in real hardware the next opcode is fetched during the previous instruction's final M-cycle, and the interrupt check happens at the end of that fetch cycle—if conditions are met, the fetched opcode gets discarded and the PC rolled back so the interrupt dispatch can take over instead.

The dispatch itself is 5 M-cycles total (per Pan Docs: wait states, two pushes, PC set). My proposal is that this discarded fetch cycle counts as the first of those 5, leaving 4 more to execute—so instead of checking for interrupts before the fetch, I check after it, letting interrupts raised during that cycle still get caught, while total dispatch timing stays unchanged at 5 M-cycles.

Working through the edge cases confirms this: whether the interrupt flag gets set during the last cycle of the prior instruction or during the fetch cycle of the next one, both the old and new models land on the handler starting at the same cycle—so the new approach doesn't change overall timing, it just shifts where the check happens.

This likely depends on sub-M-cycle T-cycle timing — where exactly within the M-cycle the timer sets IF versus when the CPU samples it, which our lumped D002 ordering doesn't capture precisely. The failing rapid_toggle test (expecting BC=FFD9 but getting FFD8) probably stems from this, so I should check that test's source along with related HALT wake and intr_timing tests.

I also need to think through the HALT case under the new model: if an interrupt is raised during a NOP's fetch cycle, dispatch starts immediately at that cycle rather than waiting for the next cycle boundary, shifting dispatch timing one cycle earlier relative to IF compared to the old model — so I need to verify this still matches the expected "HALT behaves like a NOP" semantics.

I recall older Pan Docs claimed HALT exit adds an extra 4 clocks, but the Mooneye halt_ime1_timing2-GS test suggests DMG matches NOP timing exactly, so I want to check the actual test to confirm what "same timing" means numerically. Sketching the step logic for the new model, handling the locked and halted states and checking pending interrupts...

Instead of patching this piecemeal, I'm trying a cleaner "prefetch" model closer to real hardware, where the CPU keeps an instruction register holding the already-fetched opcode: each step executes the current instruction while overlapping the fetch of the next opcode, then checks for pending interrupts after that fetch to decide whether to dispatch or continue normally.

I recall the hardware sequence: M1 fetches the opcode (discarded), M2 is an idle/decrement cycle, M3 and M4 push PCH and PCL, and M5 sets PC to the vector before the next fetch. There's still a subtlety about whether the pending-interrupt check happens before or after the peripheral tick within that fetch cycle, given the D002 ordering where peripherals tick first.

With that ordering, an interrupt flag set during cycle k is visible to the check that happens in that same fetch cycle, meaning interrupts raised up through the fetch are honored — equivalent to the old pre-fetch check but with pending state advanced by one cycle. This also clarifies the EI delay: after EI, the following NOP still sees IME=0 during its fetch check, so it executes normally, and only after that does IME become 1, meaning the interrupt can only be taken on the fetch after the NOP.

This matches the known "ei; nop" case — interrupt dispatches after the nop, confirming the BC value stays unchanged. For RETI, IME is set immediately and the next fetch checks and dispatches with the return address intact, same as before.

Now I'm tracing the HALT bug combined with pending interrupts: "EI; HALT" sets halt_bug when IME is still 0, then IME flips to 1, and the next fetch happens with PC not incremented due to the bug, triggering dispatch at that point.

I realize the uniform rule is that whenever dispatch occurs, PC should be set to one less than wherever the fetch left it — this naturally reproduces the normal case (fetch advances, dispatch rolls back one) and the halt bug case (fetch doesn't advance, dispatch still rolls back one, landing exactly on the halt instruction per Pan Docs). So the fix is to let the fetch happen normally with the halt bug intact, then on dispatch just decrement PC by one from wherever the fetch left it.

Now I need to work out HALT timing in this model: during halted idle cycles, the CPU presumably keeps re-reading the same PC without advancing, and I need the interrupt-wake timing to align with how NOPs dispatch five cycles after the interrupt flag is raised, meaning the idle cycle where IF gets raised should act as the first of those five dispatch cycles.

Then execution resumes at the following instruction fetch on the next cycle. I'm cross-checking against the documented behavior that IME=0 HALT should behave exactly like a sequence of NOPs waiting for the interrupt, timing-wise identical.

I should trace through the test cases fully to pin down exact timing expectations, examining rapid_toggle, intr_timing, di_timing, ei_timing, and halt_ime1_timing together.

Switched to a new branch 'w4/core'
; This test rapidly starts and stops the timer.
; There are two behaviours that affect the test:
;   1. starting or stopping the timer does *not* reset its internal counter,
;      so repeated starting and stopping does not prevent timer increments
;   2. the timer circuit design causes some unexpected timer increases

; Common reasons for failing this test:
;   "FAIL: NO INTR"
;     Your emulator starts counting the timer when it is started or stopped.
;     This is incorrect, because in real hardware starting/stopping the timer
;     simply flips a single bit, and the timer state is otherwise preserved.
;   BC < $FFF8
;     Your emulator does not emulate the unexpected timer increases, so the
;     interrupt happens too late.

; Verified results:
;   pass: DMG, MGB, SGB, SGB2, CGB, AGB, AGS
;   fail: -

.include "common.s"

test:
  ld a, INTR_TIMER
  ldh (<IE), a
  xor a
  ldh (<IF), a
  ldh (<DIV), a
  ld a, $F0
  ldh (<TIMA), a
  ld a, %00000100 ; Start 4096 Hz timer
  ldh (<TAC), a

  ld bc, $FFFF

  ei

- ld a, %00000100 ; Start 4096 Hz timer
  ldh (<TAC), a
  ld a, %00000000 ; Stop timer
  ldh (<TAC), a
  dec bc
  ld a, c
  or b
  jr nz, -

  quit_failure_string "FAIL: NO INTR"

test_finish:
  setup_assertions
  assert_b $FF
  assert_c $D9
  quit_check_asserts

.org INTR_VEC_TIMER
  jp test_finish

content.content:
; Serving an interrupt is supposed to take 5 M-cycles.
; We know from div_timing that this code should not see a div increment:
;   reset_div
;     nops 61
;   ld a, (hl)
; On the other hand, this code should see the increment:
;   reset_div
;     nops 62
;   ld a, (hl)
; We set up a similar scenario by triggering an interrupt using IE/IF flags.
; In total we have
;   reset_div
;     x nops               x cycles
;     trigger_intr 2 + 3 = 5 cycles
;     interrupt handling:  5 cycles
;     jp hl                1 cycle
;   ld a, (bc)
; So, x=50 is equivalent to the nops 61 case,
; and x=51 is equivalent to the nops 62 case

; Verified results:
;   pass: DMG, MGB, SGB, SGB2, CGB, AGB, AGS
;   fail: -

.include "common.s"

  ld bc, DIV

  ld a, INTR_SERIAL
  ldh (<IE), a

.macro reset_div
  xor a
  ld (bc), a
.endm

.macro trigger_intr
  ld a, $08
  ldh (<IF), a
.endm

test_round1:
  ei
  ld hl, finish_round1

  reset_div
  nops 50
  trigger_intr

  ; never executed
  quit_failure_string "FAIL: ROUND 1"

finish_round1:
  ld a, (bc)
  ld d, a

test_round2:
  ei
  ld hl, finish_round2

  reset_div
  nops 51
  trigger_intr

  ; never executed
  quit_failure_string "FAIL: ROUND 2"

finish_round2:
  ld a, (bc)
  ld e, a

  jp test_finish

test_finish:
  setup_assertions
  assert_d $00
  assert_e $01
  quit_check_asserts

.org INTR_VEC_SERIAL
  jp hl
------
; This tests DI instruction timing by setting up a vblank interrupt
; interrupt with a write to IE.
;
; This test is for DMG/MGB, so DI is expected to disable interrupts
; immediately
; On CGB/GBA DI has a delay and this test fails in round 2!!

.include "common.s"

; Verified results:
;   pass: DMG, MGB, SGB, SGB2
;   fail: CGB, AGB, AGS

  di
  ld a, INTR_VBLANK
  ldh (<IE), a

  ld hl, test_round1
  wait_vblank
  xor a
  ldh (<IF), a
  ei

  halt
  nop
  jp fail_halt

test_round1:
  ld hl, finish_round1
  ei

  delay_long_time 2505
  nops 6

  ; This DI should never get executed
  di
  jp fail_round1

finish_round1:
  ld hl, test_round2
  wait_vblank
  xor a
  ldh (<IF), a
  ei

  halt
  nop
  jp fail_halt

test_round2:
  ld hl, fail_round2
  ei

  delay_long_time 2505
  nops 5

  ; This time we let DI execute, because there is one less NOP
  di
  ; If DI doesn't have an immediate effect, we would get an interrupt here and
  ; fail the test.
  nop

test_finish:
  quit_ok

fail_halt:
  quit_failure_string "FAIL: HALT"

fail_round1:
  quit_failure_string "FAIL: ROUND 1"

fail_round2:
  quit_failure_string "FAIL: ROUND 2"

.org INTR_VEC_VBLANK
  jp hl

content.thinking:
I'm noting that rapid_toggle's failure registers all show as 0x42, which is just the standard failure marker from quit_check_asserts rather than meaningful data — so I'll ignore that detail and move on to writing a scan script that runs gb-cli across each ROM in the include set per the plan's rules.

I need to parse the final register line from each run and classify it as PASS (matching the standard success values), FAIL42 (all registers 0x42), OTHER, or NOREGS, using parallel execution via xargs. For inclusion I'm working out suffix rules — ROMs with no suffix, or suffixes containing "G" or "dmgABC" get included, while variants like -dmg0, -mgb, -S, -sgb, -cgb, -A, -C are excluded — and I'm checking a handful of example names to confirm the suffix-after-last-hyphen logic holds. Since the integrator's list already represents everything in acceptance plus emulator-only, I'll just run that full set and classify each one, then write this out as a scan script.

input.command:
cat > /tmp/core_scripts/mooneye_scan.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# mooneye_scan.sh <gb-cli> <out-file>: run every acceptance/ + emulator-only/ ROM, classify by final regs.
set -uo pipefail
CLI=$1; OUT=$2
M=/Users/skyseek/Desktop/project/open/research-platform/GB-emulator/refs/mooneye/mts-20260714-0944-31510e1
cd "$M"
one() {
  local rom=$1
  local line
  line=$(timeout 60 "$CLI" run "$rom" --until-ld-b-b --frames 1800 2>&1 | grep -E '^A=' | tail -1)
  local r
  if [ -z "$line" ]; then r=NOREGS
  elif echo "$line" | grep -q 'B=03 C=05 D=08 E=0D H=15 L=22'; then r=PASS
  elif echo "$line" | grep -q 'B=42 C=42 D=42 E=42 H=42 L=42'; then r=FAIL42
  else r=OTHER; fi
  echo "$r ${rom#./}"
}
export -f one; export CLI
find ./acceptance ./emulator-only -name '*.gb' | sort | xargs -P 6 -I{} bash -c 'one "$@"' _ {} | sort -k2 > "$OUT"
echo "PASS $(grep -c '^PASS' "$OUT") / $(wc -l < "$OUT")"
EOF
chmod +x /tmp/core_scripts/mooneye_scan.sh; cd /Users/skyseek/Desktop/project/open/research-platform/GB-emulator-lanes/core && time /tmp/core_scripts/mooneye_scan.sh $PWD/target/release/gb-cli /tmp/core_scripts/scan_base.txt; diff <(awk '{print $1, $2}' /tmp/gbemu-integrator/mooneye-scan-pre-ppu.txt) /tmp/core_scripts/scan_base.txt

I'm tracing how the TIMA overflow and subsequent IF-bit-2 set (one M-cycle after overflow, per the spec) line up with the fetch cycle of `dec bc` — under the old check-before-fetch model the interrupt would be seen one cycle late and `dec bc` would execute first, while under the new check-after-fetch model the interrupt preempts it, matching the expected behavior. Now I want to double check whether the timer's one-M-cycle overflow delay is being modeled correctly in this scenario.

Both interpretations of the timer delay seem to converge on the same outcome for this test, but I need to make sure this reasoning stays consistent with other tests like intr_timing, ei_timing, di_timing, halt tests, and the various timer tests that currently pass — starting with how intr_timing writes IF directly via `ldh (IF),a`.

content.thinking:
These halt_ime1_timing2-GS rounds depend on PPU vblank timing relative to the halt-exit point, with slightly different nop counts and DIV reset timing between the two rounds. Since the PPU lane isn't active yet in main, I can't fully resolve this dependency.

I need to keep currently passing tests passing while fixing only CPU-explainable failures. The approach is to change how halt interacts with pending interrupts: during halt, the bus idles each cycle, and if interrupts become pending after that idle, halt exits and dispatches the tail of the interrupt sequence if IME is set, matching the timing of an equivalent NOP stream where the fetch cycle is discarded and the handler fetch lands five cycles after the IF was raised. I'm checking that this aligns with the IME=0 halted case where nothing happens on IF the same way it would for a NOP stream.

For the no-interrupt timing test, I'm comparing the IME=1 case (handler dispatch of five cycles plus the one-cycle JP HL) against the IME=0 case (six NOP-equivalent cycles after wake), and reasoning that the fetch of the first instruction after wake effectively overlaps with the interrupt cycle itself, so both paths land on the same finishing cycle.

This points to a new model: treat each halted cycle as an attempted fetch of the next opcode (reading PC), so if the pending interrupt appears, the CPU can either dispatch the handler (IME on) or simply execute the opcode it just fetched (IME off) without losing a cycle, while staying halted just discards that read without advancing PC.

But I'm second-guessing whether that matches prior tests expecting halted steps to show as plain idle cycles, since reading PC from ROM/WRAM/HRAM has no observable side effects on our peek-based bus anyway. I'll likely need to keep the external "idle" label for bus-logging purposes while internally treating it as a fetch attempt.

Tracing through both timelines confirms they match: with IME=1, dispatch consumes cycles through k+5 before the handler's JP HL fetch, landing on the finish fetch at k+6; with IME=0, six NOPs fetched sequentially land on the same finish cycle. Comparing against the current implementation's model shows it would instead place the finish fetch at k+7, one cycle later — so the discard-based halted fetch model is the one that lines up correctly.

For the ldh (IF),a case, cycle k is the write cycle rather than a fetch, so the next fetch happens at k+1, and in the new model the check after that fetch at k+1 sees IF set and dispatches with k+1 as the discarded fetch. The old model instead checks right before fetch k+1, equivalent to right after cycle k, and also sees IF set, dispatching across k+1..k+5 — so both models land on the same result here too.

The real divergence only shows up when a peripheral raises IF during the tick phase of a fetch cycle itself (per D002, tick precedes access within the same cycle). For CPU-written IF there's no difference, but for peripheral-raised IF, the new model catches the interrupt one instruction earlier when it coincides with a fetch cycle's tick. Essentially the old model checks pending status as of after the previous cycle's access, while the new model also incorporates the current fetch cycle's tick phase.

These tests rely on wait_vblank, which spins on LY until it hits 144 — but with the PPU stubbed out, LY never advances, so it could loop forever. That matches what I'm seeing: the gb-cli run hits 1800 frames and reports OTHER, not 42 or fib, confirming these tests actually need a real PPU implementation to pass.

Sorting the rest: timing tests for calls, jumps, returns, resets, and OAM DMA all depend on wait_vblank, so they go in the PPU lane. The unused I/O bits and boot_hwio/serial tests are sys-lane issues unrelated to the PPU. The oam_dma sources-GS test returning NOREGS suggests gb-cli couldn't load the cart (likely MBC5), so that's a platform-lane problem along with mbc2/mbc5/multicart tests.

Items 1 and 2 are on `lane/core` (6331d72), ready to merge; you have the commit notice. Item 3 is on `w4/core` (3783e83): `rapid_toggle` now passes, and the other CPU-related Mooneye failures can't be checked until the real PPU is in main. All four checks pass on both branches: `cargo test --workspace`, SST 500/500, gates with no regression, and no lost Mooneye passes.

## 1. OAM DMA (`lane/core` 6331d72)
- **Sync:** merged main into `lane/core` first (6baccb3).
- **Timing** (`crates/core/src/dma.rs`, frozen API unchanged):
  - The FF46 write happens in M-cycle W; W+1 is a start-up delay with no copy.
  - W+2 through W+161 copy one byte per M-cycle, 160 in total.
  - `oam_blocked()` is true exactly on those 160 copy cycles.
  - Writing FF46 during a transfer restarts it after the same one-cycle delay; the old transfer keeps copying during that delay cycle.
  - Reading FF46 returns the last value written; power-up value is 0xFF.
  - This matches the Pan Docs `ret z` note: that routine's first stack read lands on W+162, just after the last DMA cycle.
- **Snapshot for Dma:** tag `DMA `; corrupt data is rejected and the state is left unchanged.
- **Tests:**
  - `tests/dma.rs` (7): copy sequence, delay, length, all source pages, restarts, blocked interval, snapshot round trip, corrupt input.
  - `tests/dma_machine.rs` (1): a small ROM copies the HRAM routine into place and runs it. It then checks OAM via `peek`, the FF46 readback, and that reading OAM during the transfer gives 0xFF.
- **Gates:** `gb-cli gates --baseline reports/baseline.json --out /tmp/gbemu-core/gates` gives `G1 12/12 G2 1/1 G3 4/4 G4 0/1`. G4 fails only because the PPU stub is still in main, and there are no REGRESSION lines.

## 2. Test-ROM names (same commit)
- Both cpu.rs comments now describe the hardware behaviour or cite Pan Docs `halt.md`.
- `git grep -niE 'acid|blargg|mooneye|cpu_instrs|pokemon|pokered' -- crates/core/src` still finds `crates/core/src/ppu.rs:8` ("Blargg"). That file belongs to the ppu lane, so I didn't touch it.

## 3. Interrupt check timing (`w4/core` 3783e83)
- **Cause:** I confirmed the sys lane's analysis against the `rapid_toggle` source. The write that stops the timer overflows TIMA in M-cycle 10 of the loop. IF is set one M-cycle later, which is the opcode-fetch cycle of `dec bc`. The old model executed `dec bc` before dispatching, giving BC=FFD8; checking after the fetch gives FFD9.
- **Change:** `step()` now fetches the opcode and then checks `IME && pending()`.
  - On dispatch the fetched opcode is thrown away and PC steps back one. After a HALT bug this lands on the HALT itself, as Pan Docs describes.
  - The discarded fetch counts as dispatch cycle 1 of 5: fetch, idle, push high byte, push low byte, idle.
  - While halted, each M-cycle is now a read at PC (PC doesn't advance) instead of an idle. On wake with IME=1 that read becomes dispatch cycle 1; with IME=0 the fetched instruction runs right away. This keeps HALT waiting exactly as fast as a NOP loop.
- **Tests:** 7 tests in `tests/cpu_interrupts.rs` encoded the old cycle shapes and were updated. I added `interrupt_raised_during_fetch_preempts_that_instruction` and a reverse case in `di_is_immediate`: an interrupt raised during DI's own fetch is taken before DI runs. The file now has 22 tests, all passing.
- **Results** (scan script `/tmp/core_scripts/mooneye_scan.sh`, which runs `gb-cli run --until-ld-b-b --frames 1800` on all 103 acceptance and emulator-only ROMs):

| | Mooneye PASS | Difference |
|---|---|---|
| Your list (pre-PPU) | 40 | |
| `lane/core` with DMA | 41 | +`oam_dma/basic` |
| `w4/core` | 42 | +`timer/rapid_toggle`, nothing lost |

  G1–G3 stay all-pass and SST stays 500/500. A 1200-frame pokered run ends in exactly the same state on `lane/core` and `w4/core` (the LY wait loop, since the PPU is still a stub).

## Open issues
- **Waiting on the PPU:** all remaining CPU-related failures use `wait_vblank`/`wait_ly`. That covers the `*_timing` tests (call, jp, ret, push, rst, add_sp_e, ld_hl_sp_e), `di_timing-GS`, `halt_ime0_*`, `halt_ime1_timing2-GS` and `oam_dma_*`. Working `push_timing` through by hand, its results should come out right once the PPU is in. I'll re-scan after main has the PPU and merge it into `w4/core`.
- **For other lanes:**
  - sys: the ignored test `oam_dma_copies_from_wram_and_echo` in `tests/bus.rs` now passes and can be un-ignored.
  - sys: the bus doesn't block CPU access outside HRAM during DMA, which Pan Docs describes.

  - platform: `oam_dma/sources-GS` needs MBC5 support.

"""Replay a driver-actions log to N requests, then probe whether the player responds to input."""
import json, sys
from gbemu.backend import GbEmuEmulator
from gbemu.replay import apply_action

log, rom, upto = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3])
emu = GbEmuEmulator(); emu.load(rom); emu.tick(60)
n = 0
with open(log) as f:
    for line in f:
        if n >= upto: break
        req = json.loads(line)
        acts = req.get("actions") or req.get("request", {}).get("actions") or []
        for a in acts: apply_action(emu, a)
        n += 1
def pos():
    return (emu.read_u8(0xD35E), emu.read_u8(0xD362), emu.read_u8(0xD361))  # map, x, y (pokered wCurMap, wXCoord, wYCoord)
print("after replay:", n, "requests; map,x,y =", pos(), "wd730=%02x" % emu.read_u8(0xD730), "joyignore(CD6B)=%02x" % emu.read_u8(0xCD6B))
for a in ["press_b", "press_b", "walk_left", "walk_left", "walk_right", "walk_right", "walk_up", "walk_down", "press_a", "wait_60", "press_a", "wait_60"]:
    apply_action(emu, a)
    print(f"{a:10s} -> map,x,y={pos()} wd730={emu.read_u8(0xD730):02x} CD6B={emu.read_u8(0xCD6B):02x} textbox={emu.read_u8(0xD125):02x}")
emu.get_screen().save("/tmp/gbemu-integrator/stall/probe-after.png")
"""Replay a log and save screenshots + key WRAM at selected request indices."""
import json, sys
from PIL import Image
from gbemu.backend import GbEmuEmulator
from gbemu.replay import apply_action
log, rom, out = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
marks = [int(x) for x in sys.argv[4].split(",")]
emu = GbEmuEmulator(); emu.load(rom); emu.tick(60)
shots = []; n = 0
reqs = [json.loads(l) for l in open(log)]
for i, req in enumerate(reqs[: max(marks) + 1]):
    if i in marks:
        img = emu.get_screen(); shots.append((i, img))
        s0 = emu.read_range(0xC100, 16); s0b = emu.read_range(0xC200, 16)
        print(i, "map,x,y=", (emu.read_u8(0xD35E), emu.read_u8(0xD362), emu.read_u8(0xD361)), "acts=", req.get("actions"),
              "spr0:", s0[:4].hex(), "spr0b:", s0b[:8].hex(), "wd730=%02x wd72d=%02x CD6B=%02x" % (emu.read_u8(0xD730), emu.read_u8(0xD72D), emu.read_u8(0xCD6B)))
    for a in req.get("actions") or []:
        apply_action(emu, a)
W = 160 * len(shots); sheet = Image.new("RGB", (W, 144 + 12), "white")
from PIL import ImageDraw
d = ImageDraw.Draw(sheet)
for k, (i, img) in enumerate(shots):
    sheet.paste(img, (160 * k, 12)); d.text((160 * k + 2, 0), str(i), fill="black")
sheet.save(out)

"""Replay to request N0, then print per-frame state through request N1 (core investigation)."""
import json, sys
from gbemu.backend import GbEmuEmulator
from gbemu.replay import apply_action
log, rom, n0, n1 = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3]), int(sys.argv[4])
reqs = [json.loads(l) for l in open(log)]
emu = GbEmuEmulator(); emu.load(rom); emu.tick(60)
for r in reqs[:n0]:
    for a in r.get("actions") or []:
        apply_action(emu, a)
def st():
    u = emu.read_u8
    s0 = emu.read_range(0xC100, 16).hex()
    s2 = emu.read_range(0xC200, 16).hex()
    return (f"f={emu.frame_count} map={u(0xD35E)} xy=({u(0xD362)},{u(0xD361)}) script={u(0xD5F0)} simIdx={u(0xCD38)} "
            f"sf5={u(0xD730):02x} joyIgn={u(0xCD6B):02x} tb={u(0xD125):02x} walk={u(0xCFC5)} mvdir={u(0xD528):02x} "
            f"held={u(0xFFB4):02x} pc={emu.regs()['pc']:04x} s0={s0[:8]} s2={s2[:8]}")
print("start", st())
frame_mode = len(sys.argv) > 5
for i in range(n0, n1):
    acts = reqs[i].get("actions") or []
    print(f"--- request {i}: {acts}")
    for a in acts:
        if not frame_mode:
            apply_action(emu, a); print(f"  {a:12s}", st()); continue
        parts = a.split("_")
        if parts[0] in ("press", "walk"):
            btn = "_".join(parts[1:])
            seq = [(btn, k) for k in range(8)] + [(None, k) for k in range(12)]
        elif parts[0] == "wait":
            seq = [(None, k) for k in range(int(parts[1]))]
        for btn, k in seq:
            # mirror backend.press: set bit, tick, clear
            if btn:
                emu._buttons_set(btn) if hasattr(emu, "_buttons_set") else None
            emu.press(btn, 1) if btn else emu.tick(1)
            print(f"  {a:10s}{k:3d}", st())
EOF

engine/overworld/movement.asm:1:UpdatePlayerSprite:
UpdatePlayerSprite:
	ld a, [wSpritePlayerStateData2WalkAnimationCounter]
	and a
	jr z, .checkIfTextBoxInFrontOfSprite
	cp $ff
	jr z, .disableSprite
	dec a
	ld [wSpritePlayerStateData2WalkAnimationCounter], a
	jr .disableSprite
; check if a text box is in front of the sprite by checking if the lower left
; background tile the sprite is standing on is greater than $5F, which is
; the maximum number for map tiles
.checkIfTextBoxInFrontOfSprite
	lda_coord 8, 9
	ldh [hTilePlayerStandingOn], a
	cp MAP_TILESET_SIZE
	jr c, .lowerLeftTileIsMapTile
.disableSprite
	ld a, $ff
	ld [wSpritePlayerStateData1ImageIndex], a
	ret
.lowerLeftTileIsMapTile
	call DetectCollisionBetweenSprites
	ld h, HIGH(wSpriteStateData1)
	ld a, [wWalkCounter]
	and a
	jr nz, .moving
	ld a, [wPlayerMovingDirection]
; check if down
	bit PLAYER_DIR_BIT_DOWN, a
	jr z, .checkIfUp
	xor a ; SPRITE_FACING_DOWN
	jr .next
.checkIfUp
	bit PLAYER_DIR_BIT_UP, a
	jr z, .checkIfLeft
	ld a, SPRITE_FACING_UP
	jr .next
.checkIfLeft
	bit PLAYER_DIR_BIT_LEFT, a
	jr z, .checkIfRight
	ld a, SPRITE_FACING_LEFT
	jr .next
.checkIfRight
	bit PLAYER_DIR_BIT_RIGHT, a
	jr z, .notMoving
	ld a, SPRITE_FACING_RIGHT
	jr .next
.notMoving
; zero the animation counters
	xor a
	ld [wSpritePlayerStateData1IntraAnimFrameCounter], a
	ld [wSpritePlayerStateData1AnimFrameCounter], a
	jr .calcImageIndex
.next
	ld [wSpritePlayerStateData1FacingDirection], a
	ld a, [wFontLoaded]
	bit BIT_FONT_LOADED, a
	jr nz, .notMoving
.moving
	ld a, [wMovementFlags]
	bit BIT_SPINNING, a
	jr nz, .skipSpriteAnim
	ldh a, [hCurrentSpriteOffset]
	add $7
	ld l, a
	ld a, [hl]
	inc a
	ld [hl], a
	cp 4
	jr nz, .calcImageIndex
	xor a
	ld [hl], a
	inc hl
	ld a, [hl]
	inc a
	and $3
	ld [hl], a
.calcImageIndex
	ld a, [wSpritePlayerStateData1AnimFrameCounter]
	ld b, a
	ld a, [wSpritePlayerStateData1FacingDirection]
	add b
	ld [wSpritePlayerStateData1ImageIndex], a
.skipSpriteAnim
; If the player is standing on a grass tile, make the player's sprite have
; lower priority than the background so that it's partially obscured by the
; grass. Only the lower half of the sprite is permitted to have the priority
; bit set by later logic.
	ldh a, [hTilePlayerStandingOn]
	ld c, a
	ld a, [wGrassTile]
	cp c
	ld a, 0
	jr nz, .next2
	ld a, OAM_PRIO
.next2
	ld [wSpritePlayerStateData2GrassPriority], a
	ret

	push bc
	push af
	ldh a, [hCurrentSpriteOffset]
	ld c, a
	pop af
	add c
	ld l, a
	pop bc
	ret

UpdateNPCSprite:
	ldh a, [hCurrentSpriteOffset]
	swap a
	dec a
	add a
	ld hl, wMapSpriteData
	add l
	ld l, a
	ld a, [hl]        ; read movement byte 2
	ld [wCurSpriteMovement2], a
	ld h, HIGH(wSpriteStateData1)
	ldh a, [hCurrentSpriteOffset]
	ld l, a
	inc l
	ld a, [hl]        ; x#SPRITESTATEDATA1_MOVEMENTSTATUS
	and a
	jp z, InitializeSpriteStatus
	call CheckSpriteAvailability
	ret c             ; don't do anything if sprite is invisible
	ld h, HIGH(wSpriteStateData1)
	ldh a, [hCurrentSpriteOffset]
	ld l, a
	inc l
	ld a, [hl]        ; x#SPRITESTATEDATA1_MOVEMENTSTATUS
	bit BIT_FACE_PLAYER, a
	jp nz, MakeNPCFacePlayer
	ld b, a
	ld a, [wFontLoaded]
	bit BIT_FONT_LOADED, a
	jp nz, NotYetMoving
	ld a, b
	cp $2
	jp z, UpdateSpriteMovementDelay  ; [x#SPRITESTATEDATA1_MOVEMENTSTATUS] == 2
	cp $3
	jp z, UpdateSpriteInWalkingAnimation  ; [x#SPRITESTATEDATA1_MOVEMENTSTATUS] == 3
	ld a, [wWalkCounter]
	and a
	ret nz           ; don't do anything yet if player is currently moving
	call InitializeSpriteScreenPosition
	ld h, HIGH(wSpriteStateData2)
	ldh a, [hCurrentSpriteOffset]
	add $6
	ld l, a
	ld a, [hl]       ; x#SPRITESTATEDATA2_MOVEMENTBYTE1
	inc a
	jr z, .randomMovement  ; value STAY
	inc a
	jr z, .randomMovement  ; value WALK
; scripted movement
	dec a
	ld [hl], a       ; increment movement byte 1 (movement data index)
	dec a
	push hl
	ld hl, wNPCNumScriptedSteps
	dec [hl]         ; decrement wNPCNumScriptedSteps
	pop hl
	ld de, wNPCMovementDirections
	call LoadDEPlusA ; a = [wNPCMovementDirections + movement byte 1]
	cp NPC_CHANGE_FACING
	jp z, ChangeFacingDirection
	cp STAY
	jr nz, .next
; reached end of wNPCMovementDirections list
	ld [hl], a ; store $ff in movement byte 1, disabling scripted movement
	ld hl, wStatusFlags5
	res BIT_SCRIPTED_NPC_MOVEMENT, [hl]
	xor a
	ld [wSimulatedJoypadStatesIndex], a
	ld [wUnusedOverrideSimulatedJoypadStatesIndex], a
	ret
.next
	cp WALK
	jr nz, .determineDirection
; current NPC movement data is WALK ($fe). this seems buggy
	ld [hl], $1     ; set movement byte 1 to $1
	ld de, wNPCMovementDirections

CheckSpriteAvailability:
	predef IsObjectHidden
	ldh a, [hIsToggleableObjectOff]
	and a
	jp nz, .spriteInvisible
	ld h, HIGH(wSpriteStateData2)
	ldh a, [hCurrentSpriteOffset]
	add SPRITESTATEDATA2_MOVEMENTBYTE1
	ld l, a
	ld a, [hl]      ; x#SPRITESTATEDATA2_MOVEMENTBYTE1
	cp WALK
	jr c, .skipXVisibilityTest ; movement byte 1 < WALK (i.e. the sprite's movement is scripted)
	ldh a, [hCurrentSpriteOffset]
	add SPRITESTATEDATA2_MAPY
	ld l, a
	ld b, [hl]      ; x#SPRITESTATEDATA2_MAPY
	ld a, [wYCoord]
	cp b
	jr z, .skipYVisibilityTest
	jr nc, .spriteInvisible ; above screen region
	add SCREEN_HEIGHT / 2 - 1
	cp b
	jr c, .spriteInvisible  ; below screen region
.skipYVisibilityTest
	inc l
	ld b, [hl]      ; x#SPRITESTATEDATA2_MAPX
	ld a, [wXCoord]
	cp b
	jr z, .skipXVisibilityTest
	jr nc, .spriteInvisible ; left of screen region
	add SCREEN_WIDTH / 2 - 1
	cp b
	jr c, .spriteInvisible  ; right of screen region
.skipXVisibilityTest
; make the sprite invisible if a text box is in front of it
; $5F is the maximum number for map tiles
	call GetTileSpriteStandsOn
	ld d, MAP_TILESET_SIZE
	ld a, [hli]
	cp d
	jr nc, .spriteInvisible ; standing on tile with ID >=MAP_TILESET_SIZE (bottom left tile)
	ld a, [hld]
	cp d
	jr nc, .spriteInvisible ; standing on tile with ID >=MAP_TILESET_SIZE (bottom right tile)
	ld bc, -SCREEN_WIDTH
	add hl, bc              ; go back one row of tiles
	ld a, [hli]
	cp d
	jr nc, .spriteInvisible ; standing on tile with ID >=MAP_TILESET_SIZE (top left tile)
	ld a, [hl]
	cp d
	jr c, .spriteVisible    ; standing on tile with ID >=MAP_TILESET_SIZE (top right tile)
.spriteInvisible
	ld h, HIGH(wSpriteStateData1)
	ldh a, [hCurrentSpriteOffset]
	add SPRITESTATEDATA1_IMAGEINDEX
	ld l, a
	ld [hl], $ff       ; x#SPRITESTATEDATA1_IMAGEINDEX
	scf
	jr .done
.spriteVisible
	ld c, a
	ld a, [wWalkCounter]
	and a
	jr nz, .done           ; if player is currently walking, we're done
	call UpdateSpriteImage
	inc h
	ldh a, [hCurrentSpriteOffset]
	add $7
	ld l, a
	ld a, [wGrassTile]

; Check whether the player did a 180-degree turn.
; It appears that this code was supposed to show the player rotate by having
; the player's sprite face an intermediate direction before facing the opposite
; direction (instead of doing an instantaneous about-face), but the intermediate
; direction is only set for a short period of time. It is unlikely for it to
; ever be visible because DelayFrame is called at the start of OverworldLoop and
; normally not enough cycles would be executed between then and the time the
; direction is set for V-blank to occur while the direction is still set.
	swap a ; put old direction in upper half
	or b ; put new direction in lower half
	cp (PLAYER_DIR_DOWN << 4) | PLAYER_DIR_UP ; change dir from down to up
	jr nz, .notDownToUp
	ld a, PLAYER_DIR_LEFT
	ld [wPlayerMovingDirection], a
	jr .holdIntermediateDirectionLoop
.notDownToUp
	cp (PLAYER_DIR_UP << 4) | PLAYER_DIR_DOWN ; change dir from up to down
	jr nz, .notUpToDown
	ld a, PLAYER_DIR_RIGHT
	ld [wPlayerMovingDirection], a
	jr .holdIntermediateDirectionLoop
.notUpToDown
	cp (PLAYER_DIR_RIGHT << 4) | PLAYER_DIR_LEFT ; change dir from right to left

content.text:
Nothing on the emulator side contradicts the scout's conclusion. I traced the stall instruction by instruction and every step is ordinary game code, so I've stopped, as you asked.

**What the trace shows:**
- **Normal frames:** the VBlank handler runs from LY 144 to about LY 40–41. `_UpdateSprites` then runs from about LY 42 to about LY 120, leaving roughly 24 lines spare.
- **Frame 185413:** the music engine starts new notes on channels 1 and 2 (it writes NR11–NR19). The time between `FadeOutAudio` and `TrackPlayTime` goes from the usual 2,600–2,900 T to about 8,600 T, so the handler ends at LY 54.
- **Frame 185414:** `_UpdateSprites` starts at LY 58. The two Pokédexes (slots 6/7) become visible at LY 110 and 117. VBlank fires at LY 144 while the loop is still running (interrupted at `pc=4cf2`, bank 1), before the scientists (slots 10/11) have been marked invisible.
- **The overflow:** `PrepareOAMData` therefore writes 11 sprites; the extra entries spill out of the 0xC300–0xC39F shadow-OAM buffer into the tile map at 0xC3A0. At frame 185415 the tile under the player (0xC45C) turns into 0xA0.
- **The lock:** afterwards, a left press is accepted (`wPlayerDirection` becomes LEFT), but a sprite-in-front check flips it back to UP each frame and the collision check blocks the move. That is consistent with the scout's self-lock.

**The three points you asked about:**
- **Frame CPU budget:** every frame is exactly 70,224 T, and the VBlank interrupt lands within 8 T of the same point each frame (t=40108–40116), whether the CPU was halted or running. During these frames the game reads only P1, DIV and NR51 from I/O, with no LY/STAT polling and no APU status bits. So how long each frame's work takes depends only on game state, not on any PPU or APU state we might emulate wrongly. Per-instruction cycle counts are the SST-verified ones.
- **HALT exit to ISR:** it is 5 M-cycles with no extra wake-up delay. That is consistent with the Mooneye `intr_timing`, `halt_ime1_timing2-GS` and `di_timing-GS` tests passing.
- **OAM DMA:** a 1 M-cycle start-up delay plus 160 M-cycles. The DMA never stalls the CPU, and the game waits it out in its HRAM loop, so the DMA adds no extra cycles to the frame.

The overrun is about 13 lines (around 6,000 T), far more than any plausible few-cycle error in the areas above.

**Repo state:** I committed nothing for this investigation. The tracers and a patched scratch copy of gb-core with an I/O read counter are only in `/tmp/core_scripts/stall/`. `git status --short` in my worktree is empty and the worktree is on lane/core. The one new commit is the routine sync merge I made before starting:
